# 1. Open Stat Prog Modules

From [Open Statistical Programming](https://www.openstatprog.com/) work on the modules:

- Pipes

- Descriptive statistics

- Reproducible reporting

- External data

# 2. Hand-in assignment

With this hand-in assignment, you demonstrate that you can set up a project as you learned during the lecture, import external data, know how to work with pipes, calculate some descriptive statistics, and know how to make a reproducible report using Quarto.

**Data:** [penguins.csv](../data/penguins.csv){download="penguins.csv"} (click to download) contains measurements of 344 penguins from the Palmer Archipelago in Antarctica. Note that the file uses **semicolons** to separate columns and **commas** as decimal marks.

::: callout-important
## What to hand in

- Hand in **only your rendered `.html` file**. Do not hand in your `.qmd` file, the data or a zip of your project.
- Name your file **`lab1_firstname_lastname_studentnumber.html`**, for example `lab1_jane_doe_1234567.html`.
- Use `embed-resources: true` in your header so that your figure is stored inside the `.html` file.
:::

## Set up your project

**Exercise 1**

Set up an R project with the same folder structure as the "good" example from the lecture (see the [Project Organization Demo](../assets/project_organization.zip)):

1.  In RStudio, create a new project called `lab1` (*File \> New Project \> New Directory \> New Project*).
2.  Inside the project folder, create the folders `code`, `data`, `figures` and `output`.
3.  [Download penguins.csv](../data/penguins.csv){download="penguins.csv"} and save it in the `data` folder.
4.  Create a new Quarto document (*File \> New File \> Quarto Document*) and save it in the `code` folder as `lab1_firstname_lastname_studentnumber.qmd`.

``` markdown
---
title: "lab1_firstname_lastname_studentnumber"
author: "Firstname Lastname"
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
---
```

Your project should now look like this:

```         
lab1/
├── lab1.Rproj
├── code/
│   └── lab1_firstname_lastname_studentnumber.qmd
├── data/
│   └── penguins.csv
├── figures/
└── output/
```

## Import the data

**Exercise 2**

Add a code chunk that loads the `dplyr` package. Then, just like in the example from the lecture, define a variable for each folder in your project:

``` r
dataDir <- "data"
outDir  <- "output"
figDir  <- "figures"
```

Read `penguins.csv` into an object called `penguins` with `read.csv2()` and `here::here(dataDir, "penguins.csv")`.

How many rows and columns does `penguins` have?

```{r, include = params$answers, message = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

dataDir <- "data"
outDir  <- "output"
figDir  <- "figures"

penguins <- read.csv2(here::here(dataDir, "penguins.csv"))

dim(penguins)  # 344 rows, 8 columns
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** The data has 344 rows and 8 columns.",
    "With `read.csv()` (instead of `read.csv2()`) you would get only 1 column,",
    "because `read.csv()` expects commas between columns.\n")
```

## Descriptive statistics with pipes

**Exercise 3**

Convert `species` into a factor with the levels `"Adelie"`, `"Chinstrap"` and `"Gentoo"` (in that order). Then use `table()` to count the penguins of each species.

```{r, include = params$answers}
penguins$species <- factor(penguins$species,
                           levels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))

table(penguins$species)
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** Adelie: 152, Chinstrap: 68, Gentoo: 124.\n")
```

**Exercise 4**

Calculate the mean body mass (`body_mass_g`) of all penguins, rounded to 1 decimal. Write this as **one pipeline** using the base R pipe `|>`. Remember that `body_mass_g` contains missing values.

```{r, include = params$answers}
penguins$body_mass_g |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  round(1)
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** 4201.8 grams. Without `na.rm = TRUE` the result is `NA`,",
    "because 2 penguins have a missing body mass.\n")
```

**Exercise 5**

Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` in a pipeline to calculate the mean body mass **per species**, rounded to 1 decimal. Which species is the heaviest on average?

```{r, include = params$answers}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = round(mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 1)) |>
  as.data.frame()  # a tibble prints fewer digits (3701 instead of 3700.7)
```

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**Answer:** Adelie: 3700.7 g, Chinstrap: 3733.1 g, Gentoo: 5076.0 g.",
    "Gentoo penguins are the heaviest on average.\n")
```

Store the result of your pipeline in an object called `mass_by_species`, and save it in your `output` folder:

```{r, include = params$answers, eval = FALSE}
mass_by_species <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = round(mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 1))

saveRDS(mass_by_species, here::here(outDir, "mass_by_species.rds"))
```

## Reproducible reporting

**Exercise 6**

Write one sentence in your document (as normal text, **not** in a code chunk) that reports the mean body mass from Exercise 4. Do not type the number yourself: use **inline code** so that the number is calculated when you render the document.

*Hint:* inline code looks like this: `` `r knitr::inline_expr("1 + 1")` ``

```{r, include = params$answers, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
mean_mass <- round(mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

cat("**Answer:** In the text of the document, write:\n\n",
    "```markdown\n",
    "The mean body mass of the penguins is `r round(mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` grams.\n",
    "```\n\n",
    "which renders as:\n\n",
    "> The mean body mass of the penguins is ", mean_mass, " grams.\n",
    sep = "")
```

**Exercise 7**

Make a boxplot of body mass per species with base R's `boxplot()` function. Add a caption to the figure with the chunk option `#| fig-cap:`, and give the axes clear labels.

```{r, include = params$answers}
#| fig-cap: "Body mass of penguins per species."
boxplot(body_mass_g ~ species,
        data = penguins,
        xlab = "Species",
        ylab = "Body mass (g)")
```

Also save the boxplot as an image in your `figures` folder. `png()` opens an image file, the plot is drawn into that file, and `dev.off()` closes it:

``` r
png(here::here(figDir, "boxplot_mass.png"))
boxplot(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins,
        xlab = "Species", ylab = "Body mass (g)")
dev.off()
```

```{r, include = params$answers, eval = FALSE}
png(here::here(figDir, "boxplot_mass.png"))
boxplot(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins,
        xlab = "Species", ylab = "Body mass (g)")
dev.off()
```

- all your code, output, your inline sentence and your boxplot show up in the `.html` file;
